issues.legal_issue: A court confirming a sale of a company’s assets in liquidation must ensure that the sale is conducted so as to realise the best possible price for the creditors.
material_facts: The sale of the company’s assets was advertised only once in three newspapers, at least two of which were local.
A valuation report had been obtained but was not disclosed to the secured creditors, and the valuation did not account for the company’s leasehold land adequately.
No reserve price was fixed, and the sale order did not state that the accepted price was fair or adequate in light of the assets’ valuation.
The successful offer proposed payment terms that differed from the published terms, and another offer was not meaningfully compared with it.

The sale order did not assess the total claims against the company or the interests of unsecured creditors, and possession was ordered to be handed over promptly despite only part of the price having been paid.
issues.conclusion: The sale was liable to be set aside because the process did not ensure that the best possible price was obtained for the benefit of the creditors; the assets had to be revalued, a reserve bid fixed, and the sale readvertised.
issues.legal_principle: Under Rule 273 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959, sales by the Official Liquidator are subject to court-approved terms and court confirmation. The confirmation requirement safeguards against an inadequate price, and the court must satisfy itself that the price is reasonable and the best that could be obtained, whether or not fraud or irregularity is alleged. The court acts as custodian of the company and its creditors, including unsecured creditors. These principles are stated in Navalkha & Sons v. Sri Ramanya Das, which relied on Gordhan Das Chuni Lal v. T. Sriman Kanthimathinatha Pillai, Rathnaswami Pillai v. Sadapathi Pillai, S. Soundarajan v. M/s Roshan & Co., and A. Subbaraya Mudaliar v. K. Sundarajan.

predicates.liquidation_sale_confirmation_appeal: An appeal concerns a court’s confirmation of a sale of a company’s assets in liquidation.
predicates.sale_publicity_inadequate: The sale was not publicised sufficiently to give potential purchasers a fair opportunity to bid.
predicates.sale_value_not_properly_assessed: The court confirmed the sale without adequately assessing the assets’ value and whether the accepted price was the best reasonably obtainable.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns confirmation of a liquidation sale and publicity was inadequate or value was not properly assessed, the sale must be set aside.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser’s possession of assets and expenditure after a liquidation sale do not prevent the sale from being set aside when the appeal is timely and the sale process was seriously defective.
material_facts: The banks had participated in proceedings leading to the sale and did not object to it at the time.
The banks appealed within the limitation period, although the appeal was not filed until after the purchaser had taken possession.
The purchaser incurred expenditure and obligations after taking possession, knowing that the appeals were pending and that the sale could be set aside.
The sale process had serious defects, and the interests of the company’s creditors, particularly unsecured creditors, were at stake.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser’s possession, expenditure, and the banks’ participation did not justify upholding the defective sale; the appellate court should have set it aside.
issues.legal_principle: The court’s obligation to protect the interests of the company’s creditors, including unsecured creditors, outweighs equities based on a purchaser’s post-sale expenditure where the sale is defective. Expenditure incurred while an appeal is pending, with knowledge of the risk that the sale may be reversed, does not make an appeal filed within limitation infructuous. The court relied on the creditor-protection principles in Navalkha & Sons v. Sri Ramanya Das.

rule.if: appeal_against_liquidation_sale and appeal_within_limitation and sale_process_seriously_defective and purchaser_incurred_costs_with_notice

predicates.appeal_against_liquidation_sale: An appeal challenges a court-approved sale of assets in liquidation.
predicates.appeal_within_limitation: The appeal was filed within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.sale_process_seriously_defective: The sale process had defects that put at risk the realisation of the best possible price for the creditors.
predicates.purchaser_incurred_costs_with_notice: The purchaser incurred expenditure or obligations while aware that an appeal against the sale was pending.

issues.definition: A timely appeal may result in a defective liquidation sale being set aside despite purchaser costs incurred with notice of the appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A sale of secured assets is not limited to the equity of redemption when the sale terms do not expressly limit what is being sold in that way.
material_facts: The sale terms described the property being sold without expressly stating that only the equity of redemption in the secured property was being sold.
The banks’ mortgage suits remained pending when the sale order was made.
issues.conclusion: The property sold was not merely the equity of redemption in the secured assets.
issues.legal_principle: The scope of a court sale is determined by its terms; if the terms do not expressly restrict the sale to the equity of redemption, the sale is not construed as selling only that interest. The Court did not decide whether the banks had otherwise given up their securities, leaving that question to the High Court on appropriate applications.

predicates.court_sale_of_secured_property: A court sale concerns property subject to secured creditors’ interests.
predicates.sale_terms_do_not_limit_sale_to_equity_o: The terms of sale do not expressly state that only the equity of redemption is being sold.

issues.definition: When a court sells secured property and the sale terms do not limit the sale to the equity of redemption, the sale is not construed as limited to that interest.

issues.legal_issue: A lease obtained as a consequence of a court sale must be set aside when the sale itself is set aside.
material_facts: The purchaser’s associated company obtained a lease of the property to continue operating the mill after the sale.
The lease was obtained as a consequence of the sale in favour of the purchaser.
issues.conclusion: The consequential lease was also set aside.
issues.legal_principle: When a court sale is set aside, consequential arrangements founded on that sale may also be set aside to do complete justice.

predicates.liquidation_sale_set_aside: The court has set aside the sale of assets in liquidation.
predicates.lease_obtained_as_consequence_of_sale: A lease was obtained as a consequence of the sale being set aside.

issues.definition: When a liquidation sale is set aside and a lease was obtained as a consequence of that sale, the consequential lease must also be set aside.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser whose liquidation sale is set aside is entitled to repayment of the purchase price after possession is recovered, while recovery of other expenditure requires a separate application and proof of legal entitlement.
material_facts: The sale was set aside and the Official Liquidator was directed to recover possession of the assets.
The purchaser had paid the purchase price and claimed repayment of that price and other expenditure incurred after the sale.
issues.conclusion: The Official Liquidator had to repay the purchase price after recovering possession; the purchaser could recover any other expenditure only by applying to the High Court and establishing both that it had been incurred and that recovery was legally available.
issues.legal_principle: Rescission of a sale requires repayment of the purchase price, but recovery of additional expenditure depends on proof that it was incurred and that the claimant is legally entitled to recover it.

predicates.liquidation_sale_set_aside: The court has set aside the sale of assets in liquidation.
predicates.purchaser_paid_purchase_price: The purchaser paid a purchase price under the sale that was set aside.

issues.definition: When a liquidation sale is set aside and the purchaser paid the price, the price must be repaid after possession is recovered.
